Real-server failure scenarios: a revoked token is replaced by the auth provider on the next attempt; a rejected token fails with the server's data and connects after renewal; losing the network during the upgrade reconnects cleanly; an emit interrupted during a polling POST is retried after reconnecting; an acknowledgement lost with the connection fails or is retried, never both; waking after the heartbeat deadline gives exactly one disconnect and one reconnect; a full send buffer rejects the new emit without evicting accepted ones; 150 connect/disconnect cycles all connect (socket.io-client-java #289).

Stalled and trickling handshakes and stalled POSTs time out instead of hanging; messages close to maxPayload arrive intact on polling, WebSocket and after the upgrade; bursts of large WebSocket emits are paced below OkHttp's 16 MiB queue instead of closing the connection (socket.io-client-java #773/#726), and a single larger message fails with a transport error naming the limit; heartbeats keep an idle connection alive; one smoke scenario connects, emits and acknowledges over every transport mode.

HTTPS and WSS against a private CA connect only with that CA trusted; the system trust store, an expired certificate and a host name mismatch are rejected; public-key pins accept a matching key and reject others; a client certificate is presented for mutual TLS, and adding one keeps the system trust store; invalid policies are rejected when built. Adding pins to a pinned host keeps the existing ones, so a backup pin does not drop the live key.

The OkHttp stack sends headers and bodies, reports error statuses, bounds response bodies while reading, applies the request timeout but no read timeout (long polls wait), never follows an HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect, exchanges WebSocket frames and reports the close and a failed handshake's status, offers permessage-deflate only when compression is enabled, is discovered through ServiceLoader, and reports a dropped connection as a failure; the `okHttp { }` builder applies the base client and every `configure` block. A request or WebSocket OkHttp cannot build (a header value or URL it refuses) fails through the callback instead of throwing.

Engine behaviour beyond the upstream titles: pings are answered and missing pings close with `ping timeout`, a server ping resets the deadline, an invalid handshake is rejected, default path and query follow JavaScript, closing polling sends the close packet, the network-lost hook closes with `transport close`; the upgrade buffers packets and waits for a pending POST, a failed probe keeps polling and reports `upgradeError`, `upgrade: false` stays on polling; invalid cookies are ignored; POST bodies are UTF-8; query components are encoded like `encodeURIComponent`. Hostile handshakes (not JSON, wrong types, missing or negative values, values above the configured limits) end in a `transport error` close; an unknown transport name, a transport factory that throws and a throwing packet observer end in events, never in escaping exceptions; an undecodable frame is a `server error` with code `parser error`, as in JavaScript. A request the HTTP stack cannot start, before or after the handshake, is a transport error and never an exception; the cookie jar ignores cookies that are not printable ASCII. A Max-Age beyond the date range never expires instead of failing. With tryAllTransports a rejected handshake closes the polling transport before WebSocket is tried; closing a WebSocket that is still connecting cancels it, an open one closes with 1000.

Hostile peer input: 20,000 seeded malformed inputs and random text only ever fail with parse errors; known malformed headers are rejected; random values round-trip through encoder and decoder and encoder output is always decodable; ack ids outside the safe-integer range, excessive text, depth and attachment counts are rejected; a throwing reviver makes the payload invalid; attachments are numbered in JavaScript traversal order; the Engine.IO codec stops at the first error packet, decodes Base64 as leniently as Node, copies binary defensively and survives arbitrary chunk boundaries. Deeply nested payloads, which the iterative parser accepts, convert to kotlinx.serialization trees and back without recursion. A declared attachment count reserves no memory up front.

The value model behaves like JavaScript JSON: numbers print like `Number.prototype.toString`, integers stay exact, strings escape like `JSON.stringify`, parsing accepts and rejects what `JSON.parse` does, object keys order like JavaScript (duplicate keys keep the first position and the last value), deep nesting parses and prints without recursion, revivers run bottom-up, `Number()` coercion matches; Kotlin and Java values (including dates as ISO strings) convert both ways, unsupported types are rejected, values are immutable; org.json payloads convert, including primitive arrays inside them (socket.io-client-java #743); kotlinx.serialization classes round-trip; the emit, listener and acknowledgement helpers send encoded objects with the given `Json`, decode acknowledgements and events, keep emitter flags (timeouts), route undecodable payloads to `onError` or the listener error handler without stopping later events, and report decode failures and timeouts through `serializableAck`.

Lincheck proves the protocol executor and the listener registry linearizable; many threads emitting with acknowledgements lose and duplicate nothing; concurrent connect and disconnect end in a consistent state. A coroutine on another dispatcher, such as a listener callback on the callback dispatcher or a provider's withContext, is not on the executor, so what it calls is queued there instead of running inline. nextTick runs right after the current task, before work queued earlier, like a JavaScript microtask. Work a stopped executor can no longer run is reported to the caller instead of being dropped silently.

Kotlin API contracts: `emitWithAck` returns every argument and cancelling it withdraws the acknowledgement, the buffered packet and the retry entry; timed-out buffered emits leave the buffer; server acknowledgement requests are answered once and unknown ack ids ignored; reserved names and unsupported arguments fail synchronously; the auth provider runs before every connect, a throwing provider fails the attempt, late results are dropped and a slow provider delays only its namespace; buffer limits reject new emits and an overfull receive buffer or an incomplete binary packet past its deadline closes the connection; once/off/any listeners, lifecycle events, flows and outgoing interceptors behave as documented; the retry queue reads acknowledgements err-first and volatile emits bypass it; recovery replays missed events, takes offsets only from plain events and merges user auth after pid and offset; the manager caps backoff (and keeps it at the maximum where JavaScript's degenerates to 0 ms after about 1,024 attempts), emits one close, defers reconnection while offline, honours `reconnectNow`, isolates listener exceptions, shares one connection and closes it with the last socket; setup blocks run once; a missing HTTP stack is a connect error. The JavaScript Manager API: runtime reconnection setters take effect on the next attempt and validate their input, switching reconnection off stops a pending attempt, the connect timeout ends a handshake that never completes, `open(callback)` reports once without reconnecting; `pause`/`resume`, `onNetworkLost`, balanced tracer sections, the callback dispatcher, logged listener exceptions. A server-side disconnect ends the session without reconnecting; CONNECT_ERROR payloads follow socket.io-parser (text is the message, null is a parse error); byte limits of the receive buffer and retry queue; incoming acknowledgements answer once; `send`, `open`, `removeAllListeners`, emitter flag chaining, partial interceptors and `SocketIO.connect`. A provider that times out on its own (withTimeout) fails the attempt with connect_error. A packet decoded before a close that was already queued is handled before the close. close() is final without hanging anyone: acknowledgements that can no longer arrive fail with SocketDisconnectedException, the last packets are sent before the executor stops (within a grace period), calls after close() fail, callbacks queued while closing still arrive, and SocketIO.io() replaces a closed manager; open(callback) on a paused manager reports an error. Errors from listeners and a throwing listenerErrorHandler stay isolated; the setup block sees and keeps reconnection settings; a rejected emit is a manager error, not a connect_error; disconnecting cancels a provider that is still running.

Android integration under Robolectric: losing the network closes at once and its return reconnects without backoff; a new default network moves the connection; the background policy pauses and resumes, and coming back before the delay keeps the connection; the logger is gated by `Log.isLoggable`; the clock is `elapsedRealtime` and keeps counting in sleep; org.json values convert both ways and large, deep JSON streams with JsonReader; the configuration saves and restores; trim-memory releases idle connections; the Android options configure the manager; the KeyChain key manager serves only its alias. Starting without a network spends no reconnection attempts until one arrives; capability changes of the current network update `metered`/`validated`; the Android OkHttp stack (network-bound sockets and DNS, traffic tag, `configureOkHttp`) carries real requests; long trace section names never reach Trace; the streaming reader keeps every JSON type; a VPN default network is left unbound and a failed bound lookup falls back to the system resolver (issue #1). Deep payloads convert to and from org.json without recursion.

excluded_unsupported_features.reason: Android and the JVM provide no WebTransport API (no HTTP/3 WebTransport sessions in OkHttp or the platform). The client offers polling and WebSocket; the stream framing that WebTransport uses is still ported and tested (JS-287..JS-311).
